I am 70 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou since I was 20. My farm is 5 mu, and I plant cotton — it is what this soil knows best. My household has four mouths, and though my back is not what it used to be, we get by. I have a well, and out here on the North China Plain, that well is worth more than gold when the dry winds blow.

This year, I will put all 5 mu into cotton. I will buy improved seeds from the county supply station — the kind with bollworm resistance bred in. I have learned over the years that these seeds save money because they cut the pesticide bill. In mid-April, when the soil warms, I will rotary-till the fields to break up the ground and bury last year’s stubble. Then I will lay down my fertilizer: about 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 12 kg of potassium per mu. Cotton is hungry, especially when the bolls start forming, and I know this land needs feeding.

I will irrigate four times using my well: once right after sowing to settle the seeds, once at flowering, once when the bolls are setting, and a fourth time in late summer if the heat is cruel and the skies stay empty. Even with resistant seeds, I will spray pesticides five times — aphids and spider mites do not rest, and neither will I. By autumn, if the weather holds and no big storm flattens the field, I expect to bring in about 250 kg of seed cotton per mu. That is enough to keep the household warm and fed.
